title: Climbing Fixed Ladders to Rooftop Units: Keep Your Hands Free
summary: An air conditioning technician died after falling about 25 feet from a 13-foot fixed ladder to a roof hatch while climbing with a heavy valve in his hand. Plan how you get tools up, and check the ladder and hatch before you climb.
talking_points: In this case, a 58-year-old technician fell from a fixed ladder to a roof hatch. No one saw the fall, so the exact cause is unknown. He may have lost balance carrying a heavy valve, dropped it and lost his footing, or twisted at the top to get around a hatch that was installed backward.
Use caution every time you climb or work from a ladder. Face the ladder and keep three points of contact.
Do not carry tools or parts in your hands while climbing. Use a hoist line, bucket, or tool belt, or have a coworker raise them.
Check the ladder and the roof hatch before you climb. A hatch that opens toward you at the top can force you to twist and let go. Report it and do not climb it until it is safe.
Plan trips to the truck. Bring the parts and gauges you need to the roof in one safe lift instead of making many climbs.
Do a job hazard analysis with the crew each day before work. Look at fall hazards, loose debris, electrical hazards, and weather. This day was hot and sunny.
Employers must train workers to recognize ladder hazards and the steps to reduce them (29 CFR 1926.1060).
site_hazards_to_check: Fixed ladder rungs, side rails, or hatch that are damaged or poorly installed
Roof hatch that opens toward the climber and blocks a safe step-off
Open drop beside the stairs or landing below the ladder
Unguarded skylights and roof openings near the rooftop units
Equipment left on landings or stairs
discussion_questions: How will each person get tools, gauges, and parts to the roof without carrying them up the ladder?
What did you check on the ladder and hatch before climbing?
What fall hazards are on the roof today besides the ladder?
